title: MTRX™ Field Series No. 06 · Read the room · Kevin Cecil

cards.name: Why this guide exists
cards.q: What does this guide treat every read of a person as?
options: A verdict you can act on
A hypothesis you test by asking
cards.why: Notice, guess, ask, update. A read you never check is just a story you like.

cards.name: Why this guide exists
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Why this guide exists" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I don't read minds. I read changes, then I ask."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: In real time, how often do people correctly judge whether someone is lying or telling the truth?
cards.why: Bond and DePaulo 2006, 24,483 judges: 54%. Stop 1.1.

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: Compared with students, how good are police and other professionals at spotting lies?
cards.why: About 54.5% vs 54.1% (Aamodt and Custer 2006). Stop 1.1.

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: "Communication is 7% words, 38% tone and 55% body language." That rule is...
options: A narrow 1967 result about feelings when words and tone clash
cards.why: Mehrabian rejects the general use. Stop 1.4.

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: Someone looks up and to the right while answering. That tells you...
cards.why: The NLP eye claim failed in three studies (Wiseman et al. 2012). Stop 1.3.

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: A clinic owner sounds nervous on your call. Most likely meaning?
options: Nothing specific: stress has many causes
cards.why: Reading stress as lying is the Othello error. Stop 1.3.

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: Best way to understand what a client wants?
options: Imagine yourself in their shoes, carefully
cards.why: Across 25 experiments, asking beat imagining (Eyal, Steffel and Epley 2018). Stop 1.8.

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: After a first conversation, people usually like you...
options: About as much as you think
cards.why: The liking gap (Boothby et al. 2018). Stop 1.11.

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: When you're nervous presenting, how visible is it?
options: Exactly as visible as it feels
cards.why: The illusion of transparency (Gilovich et al. 1998). Stop 1.11.

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: A psychic says "you're independent, but sometimes you doubt yourself" and it feels spot on. Why?
cards.why: A Barnum statement. Stop 1.9.

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: Which trait do strangers judge most accurately from a first impression?
cards.why: Visible traits read best (Borkenau and Liebler 1992). Stop 1.2.

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Your baseline: ten questions first" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I tested my instincts before I trusted them."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The 54% problem
cards.q: Across 24,483 judges, what was the average accuracy at telling lies from truths in real time?
cards.why: Bond and DePaulo 2006. Lies were caught 47% of the time, truths 61%: we lean toward believing.

cards.name: The 54% problem
cards.q: Your caller is 'sure' a clinic owner lied about having no budget. What does research say about that sureness?
cards.why: DePaulo et al. 1997. Check the budget with a question, not a gut call.

cards.name: The 54% problem
cards.q: Why did Bond's read of Le Chiffre's tell cost him?
options: A visible tell can be faked by someone who knows you're watching
cards.why: A cue you can see, the other side can plant. Treat it as a hypothesis to test.

cards.name: The 54% problem
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The 54% problem" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Most people can't spot a lie much better than a coin flip, so I don't guess. I ask and I check."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: First impressions: fast, sticky, half right
cards.q: People shown a face for 100 milliseconds...
options: Form impressions that match their unlimited-time judgments
Are more accurate than with longer looks
cards.why: Willis and Todorov 2006. Longer looks mostly raise confidence, not accuracy.

cards.name: First impressions: fast, sticky, half right
cards.q: Which trait do strangers judge most accurately at first sight?
cards.why: Visible traits leak into behaviour; honesty and intelligence mostly don't (Borkenau and Liebler 1992).

cards.name: First impressions: fast, sticky, half right
cards.q: A safari operator sounds cold for the first 30 seconds of a call. Best move?
options: Note it as a guess and keep gathering
cards.why: Thin slices carry some signal and a lot of noise. Let later behaviour update the read.

cards.name: First impressions: fast, sticky, half right
cards.q: Page closed: explain "First impressions: fast, sticky, half right" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "First impressions are fast and they agree with each other. That doesn't make them right, so I hold mine loosely."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Baselines: read the change, not the tell
cards.q: In DePaulo's meta-analysis of 158 possible lie cues, what did they find?
options: A few cues reliably reveal lies
Most cues are weak or unrelated to lying
Eye contact is the best cue
cards.why: 1,338 estimates, 120 samples. There is no single tell.

cards.name: Baselines: read the change, not the tell
cards.q: A clinic owner tenses up when you ask about his current website. Most defensible read?
options: He wants to end the call
The topic matters to him somehow: ask
cards.why: Stress has many causes. Reading it as lying is the Othello error. Name it and ask.

cards.name: Baselines: read the change, not the tell
cards.q: Why did the three fingers give Hicox away?
options: He held eye contact too long
It broke the German way of counting from the thumb
cards.why: A culture mismatch, not a lie cue. Context is part of every baseline.

cards.name: Baselines: read the change, not the tell
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Baselines: read the change, not the tell" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I don't trust tells. I watch for change from someone's normal, and then I ask about it."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The five channels
cards.q: The '7% words, 38% tone, 55% body' rule is...
options: A narrow 1967 finding about feelings when words and tone conflict
cards.why: Mehrabian's studies used single words about liking. He rejects the general use.

cards.name: The five channels
cards.q: For catching deception, training on which channel works better?
cards.why: Hauch et al. 2014: verbal content training had the larger effects.

cards.name: The five channels
cards.q: A prospect says 'sounds good' after a long pause, in a flat voice, then changes topic. Best move?
options: Trust the words, ignore the rest
Ask about the gap between words and tone
cards.why: When channels disagree, ask. 'Sounds good, or sounds like a lot?'

cards.name: The five channels
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The five channels" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Words carry more than people think. I listen to what someone chooses to say, then check it against how they say it."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Warmth first, then competence
cards.q: In the warmth and competence research, which tends to weigh more in overall impressions?
cards.why: Warmth (intent) comes first and weighs more (Wojciszke 1998; Fiske et al. 2007).

cards.name: Warmth first, then competence
cards.q: Babyfaced adults tend to be seen as...
options: Warmer but less powerful and competent
cards.why: Zebrowitz 2017. The job is showing competence: proof, pace, preparation.

cards.name: Warmth first, then competence
cards.q: Which competence signal has evidence behind it but does NOT prove real ability?
cards.why: Speaking time predicts who emerges as leader, not who leads well. Use real proof too.

cards.name: Warmth first, then competence
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Warmth first, then competence" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "People decide if you're on their side before they decide if you're good. So I show I care first, then I show proof."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: What people want
cards.q: Asking a prospect for advice tends to make you look...
options: More competent, especially on hard questions
cards.why: Brooks, Gino and Schweitzer 2015.

cards.name: What people want
cards.q: In ultimatum games, why do people turn down free money?
options: They reject unfair offers even at a cost
cards.why: Fairness is a want you can't ignore, especially in pricing.

cards.name: What people want
cards.q: A clinic owner says 'my last agency took my money and vanished'. Which want is loudest?
cards.why: Fairness. Answer it head on: milestones, what he owns, how he can leave.

cards.name: What people want
cards.q: Page closed: explain "What people want" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Most people aren't buying the website. They're buying respect, control or a fair deal, so I listen for which one."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Reading power in a room
cards.q: Cheng et al. 2013 found two routes to status. Which pair?
cards.why: Dominance works through fear, prestige through respected expertise. Both raise influence.

cards.name: Reading power in a room
cards.q: Per eye-tracking research, the best clue to who holds status in a meeting is...
options: Who others look at, beyond who's speaking
cards.why: Foulsham et al. 2010: high-status people get looked at more often and for longer.

cards.name: Reading power in a room
cards.q: The famous claim that power makes people worse at perspective taking...
options: Failed a large replication for the sarcasm task
cards.why: Many Labs 3: 2,969 people, d = .03 vs the original .77.

cards.name: Reading power in a room
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Reading power in a room" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I don't look for the loudest person. I watch where the eyes go when something important is said."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Ask, don't guess
cards.q: Across 25 experiments, what improved accuracy about another person's mind?
cards.why: Eyal, Steffel and Epley 2018: perspective getting, not taking.

cards.name: Ask, don't guess
cards.q: Which questions most increased liking in Huang et al. 2017?
cards.why: Follow-ups show you listened (d = .35).

cards.name: Ask, don't guess
cards.q: You know websites; a dentist doesn't. Which bias makes you overestimate what he understands?
cards.why: Once you know something, it's hard to imagine not knowing it. Check with a question.

cards.name: Ask, don't guess
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Ask, don't guess" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I'd rather ask one good question than guess right. Guessing feels smart; asking actually is."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Cold reading, decoded
cards.q: In Forer's demonstration, 39 students got the same sketch. How accurate did they rate it?
cards.why: About 4.26 of 5. Vague, flattering statements fit nearly everyone.

cards.name: Cold reading, decoded
cards.q: 'You can be outgoing, but you also need time alone.' Which technique?
cards.why: A trait and its opposite can't miss.

cards.name: Cold reading, decoded
cards.q: What's the honest twin of a cold read?
options: An observation turned into a question you verify
cards.why: Same observation, checked instead of faked.

cards.name: Cold reading, decoded
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Cold reading, decoded" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "If a read would fit almost anyone, it isn't a read. I turn my guesses into questions."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Reading the phone and the DM
cards.q: Recruiters heard or read the same pitches. Hearing them led to...
options: Higher ratings of intellect and hireability
cards.why: Schroeder and Epley 2015: intellect effect d = 1.16 for recruiters.

cards.name: Reading the phone and the DM
cards.q: Why do sarcastic emails misfire more than senders expect?
options: Senders hear their own tone; readers don't
cards.why: Kruger et al. 2005: egocentrism over email.

cards.name: Reading the phone and the DM
cards.q: A safari operator takes six hours to reply. What does the evidence say this means?
cards.why: Reply time isn't a validated signal. Follow up on substance.

cards.name: Reading the phone and the DM
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Reading the phone and the DM" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Text loses tone, so anything warm goes in a voice note and anything important gets a direct question."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: How you read to others
cards.q: Speakers told about the illusion of transparency before a speech...
options: Were more composed and gave better speeches
cards.why: Savitsky and Gilovich 2003.

cards.name: How you read to others
cards.q: After a first conversation, people usually...
options: Overestimate how much they were liked
Underestimate how much they were liked
cards.why: The liking gap (Boothby et al. 2018).

cards.name: How you read to others
cards.q: Saying 'I'm not sure, let me check' to a client is judged...
options: More harshly by you than by them
cards.why: The beautiful mess effect (Bruk et al. 2018).

cards.name: How you read to others
cards.q: Page closed: explain "How you read to others" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "My nerves are louder inside my head than on my face. People notice far less than I fear."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The calibration log
cards.q: When can you trust a gut call, per Kahneman and Klein 2009?
options: In regular settings with lots of practice and fast, clear feedback
cards.why: Confidence isn't the test. Regularity plus feedback is.

cards.name: The calibration log
cards.q: You said 90% a prospect would book; they didn't. Your Brier score for it?
cards.why: (0.9 minus 0) squared = 0.81. Overconfidence gets punished, which is the point.

cards.name: The calibration log
cards.q: Which feedback improved forecasters most (Lichtenstein and Fischhoff 1980)?
options: How often their 70% calls came true
cards.why: Calibration feedback works; outcome-only feedback barely does.

cards.name: The calibration log
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The calibration log" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I write down my read before the meeting and score it after. That's the only way a gut gets better."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The Spotlight
cards.q: In Tamir and Mitchell 2012, how much of their possible earnings did people give up to talk about themselves?
cards.why: 17%. Talking about yourself is rewarding enough that people pay for it.

cards.name: The Spotlight
cards.q: What made Kennedy's Paris opener work?
options: He spoke fast to fill the room
He made his wife the star and himself the side character
cards.why: He named the room's favourite, cast himself as her plus-one, then thanked his hosts.

cards.name: The Spotlight
cards.q: The "70 to 80% eye contact" rule...
options: Comes from a study of Kennedy
Has no source; people prefer gaze in bouts of about 3 seconds
cards.why: Binetti et al. 2016: preferred mutual gaze averaged 3.3 seconds and varied a lot.

cards.name: The Spotlight
cards.q: Drill "The light handoff": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Name the star in your first sentence. 2) Cast yourself as the side character in one light line. 3) End with a question that puts them back on stage. Usual mistake: Self-deprecating so hard you look small. One light line, then competence.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: The Spotlight
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The Spotlight" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Charm isn't being interesting, it's making the other person feel interesting. I hand them the light first, then I talk shop."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The Name
cards.q: Why is a name harder to remember than a job (the Baker/baker paradox)?
options: A name connects to nothing you know; a job connects to lots
cards.why: McWeeny et al. 1987. Give the name meaning and recall improves (Cohen 1990).

cards.name: The Name
cards.q: In Howard, Gengler and Jain 1995, remembering someone's name...
options: Raised compliance with a purchase request
cards.why: It worked like a compliment. Forgetting did not lower compliance.

cards.name: The Name
cards.q: Miranda calling Andy "Emily" shows...
cards.why: Refusing to learn a name is how fiction, and bad bosses, signal you are interchangeable.

cards.name: The Name
cards.q: Drill "Catch, link, keep": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Say the name back on the first hear; ask the spelling if it is unusual. 2) Link it to an image, a friend with the same name, or their business. 3) Write it with one detail within the hour, then use it once at goodbye. Usual mistake: Saying it ten times like a sales script. Hello, goodbye, maybe once in the middle.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: The Name
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The Name" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Names are hard for everyone because they mean nothing. So I make them mean something: say it back, link it, write it down. Remembering a name is the cheapest respect there is."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The Second Question
cards.q: Speed daters who did what got more second-date yeses?
cards.why: Huang et al. 2017. And people did not predict it.

cards.name: The Second Question
cards.q: You ask "How was your weekend?" then say "Mine was amazing!" Researchers call this...
cards.why: Brooks and Yeomans 2025: it reads as insincere, even though askers think it is fine.

cards.name: The Second Question
cards.q: Which closing question surfaced the most unmet concerns in a clinic trial?
options: "Is there something else you want to address today?"
cards.why: Heritage et al. 2007: "something" eliminated 78% of unmet concerns; "anything" did no better than not asking.

cards.name: The Second Question
cards.q: Drill "Three deep": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Ask a door question about them. 2) Ask about their last answer. 3) Ask one more about that answer. 4) Close with "Is there something else...?" Usual mistake: Boomerasking: asking so you can tell your own story.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: The Second Question
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The Second Question" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "The first question is manners. The second one is interest. I go three deep before I pitch, so my pitch is built from their words."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The Support Response
cards.q: "I feel lousy today." "Same here, I barely slept." This is a...
cards.why: Derber's shift response: the attention moves to you.

cards.name: The Support Response
cards.q: In Gable et al. 2004, which response to good news went with better relationships?
options: Pointing out a risk, to be helpful
cards.why: Active-constructive. The quiet version did not carry the benefit.

cards.name: The Support Response
cards.q: Peggy wants thanks; Don says "That's what the money is for!" What did he miss?
cards.why: A bid for recognition answered with logistics is a destructive response.

cards.name: The Support Response
cards.q: Drill "Ball in their court": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Match the energy of their news. 2) Ask them to relive it: how, who, what did they say. 3) If you relate, one line, then hand it back with a question. Usual mistake: The one-word "congrats", then straight to your own topic.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: The Support Response
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The Support Response" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "When someone tells me good news, I don't say 'nice' and move on. I ask how they pulled it off. Keeping the ball in their court is the whole trick."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The Compliment
cards.q: People who wrote genuine compliments predicted the recipient's reaction. They...
options: Underestimated how good it felt and overestimated the awkwardness
cards.why: Zhao and Epley 2021, nine experiments.

cards.name: The Compliment
cards.q: Why does Melvin's "better man" line land?
options: It names her effect on him, and it cost him to say it
cards.why: Effect beats adjectives, and it reveals something he would rather hide.

cards.name: The Compliment
cards.q: Kennedy's "...when Thomas Jefferson dined alone" line is an example of...
options: Praising the room inside a joke
cards.why: A compliment to everyone present, wrapped so no one had to answer. His files hold speechwriter drafts: charm can be prepared.

cards.name: The Compliment
cards.q: Drill "Change, not trait": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Name the specific action. 2) Credit the choice or effort, not looks or talent. 3) Say the impact on you or others. 4) Stop. No request attached. Usual mistake: Generic praise ("great job") or a compliment that is really a setup for a request.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: The Compliment
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The Compliment" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I don't compliment looks, I compliment choices: what someone did and what it changed. And I never attach a request to it."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The Callback
cards.q: By 1980, roughly how many names were in Clinton's card file, per Maraniss?
cards.why: Each card logged their conversations and when they got a "Glad to Meet You" letter.

cards.name: The Callback
cards.q: After a networking event, forgetting is usually...
options: Steep in the first hours and day, then slower
cards.why: Ebbinghaus's curve, replicated by Murre and Dros 2015. Write it down that night.

cards.name: The Callback
cards.q: Clinton's 1992 answer worked mainly because he...
options: Asked her to say more, then answered with people he knew by name
cards.why: A question first, then a callback to real people.

cards.name: The Callback
cards.q: Drill "The ten-minute card": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Within ten minutes: name, where you met, one personal and one business detail. 2) Set a next-touch date tied to a detail. 3) Open the next message with the callback. Usual mistake: Collecting cards and never calling back. A file you never use is just guilt.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: The Callback
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The Callback" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Memory is a system, not a gift. I write one personal and one business detail within ten minutes, and my next message opens with it. People remember the person who remembered."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Boss fight: Spotlight night
cards.q: "Guilty, I make the websites. But Rhea's the reason I'm here, ask her about her clinic." Which move?
cards.why: Stop 2.1: one light line about you, then the light goes to her.

cards.name: Boss fight: Spotlight night
cards.q: "How was your weekend?" ... "Mine was amazing, I went to..." Which mistake?
cards.why: Stop 2.3: the question was only a launchpad for your own story.

cards.name: Boss fight: Spotlight night
cards.q: You meet 12 people at an event. When should you write the cards?
options: Within the hour, before the steep part of forgetting
cards.why: Stop 2.6: forgetting is front-loaded.

cards.name: Boss fight: Spotlight night
cards.q: Drill "Spotlight night": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Hand the light on arrival. 2) Catch three names and go three deep once. 3) Answer good news actively, give one specific compliment, write the cards within the hour. Usual mistake: Running all six moves on one person. Spread them across the room.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Boss fight: Spotlight night
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Boss fight: Spotlight night" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I walk in planning to learn three names and one story, not to be impressive. Somehow that is exactly what makes people remember me."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The hungers, rebuilt: what does this person actually want?
cards.q: Which question moves most directly from a stated outcome to a deeper motive?
options: What would the result let you do?
What exact pages do you want for launch?
What colour and shape should the buttons be?
cards.why: Consequences expose what the stated object is for. Treat the answer as a hypothesis and check it.

cards.name: The hungers, rebuilt: what does this person actually want?
cards.q: Which is the SDT trio?
cards.why: Ryan and Deci identify autonomy, competence and relatedness as basic psychological needs.

cards.name: The hungers, rebuilt: what does this person actually want?
cards.q: What is wrong with the familiar Maslow pyramid?
options: Needs do not affect work or business decisions
People only want physical comfort before anything else
Maslow never drew it and the fixed staircase lacks strong support in management teaching
cards.why: The pyramid was a later graphic. Use a dynamic needs map instead.

cards.name: The hungers, rebuilt: what does this person actually want?
cards.q: Drill "The hunger ladder": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Write one stated want from a real call. 2) Write three possible needs underneath it, without choosing one yet. 3) Write one question and one tradeoff that could disconfirm each hypothesis. Usual mistake: Treating a motive label as a diagnosis. It is a question generator, not a verdict.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: The hungers, rebuilt: what does this person actually want?
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The hungers, rebuilt: what does this person actually want?" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: I do not ask what people want as if there is one answer. I ask what the result would change, then I test the read with a real choice.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The director's read: how Kazan and Lumet read actors
cards.q: Which is a playable actor direction?
options: Make your father accept this gift
Be much more visibly heartbroken in this take
Give the audience a bigger cry right now
cards.why: An action has an object and an obstacle. Emotion can arrive through the attempt.

cards.name: The director's read: how Kazan and Lumet read actors
cards.q: Why did Kazan treat Brando and Dean differently?
options: Dean was never allowed to improvise on set
Every actor must use a different camera setup and visual style for each scene
He adapted to their needs, technique and condition
cards.why: The point is adaptive direction, not a single Method formula.

cards.name: The director's read: how Kazan and Lumet read actors
cards.q: What does Lumet put under the director's responsibility?
options: Guarantee every take is perfect for the audience and critics
Keep actors from asking difficult questions
Make actors secure enough to risk self-revelation
cards.why: Lumet links good work with security and less fear, while accepting the pain of self-revelation.

cards.name: The director's read: how Kazan and Lumet read actors
cards.q: Drill "The playable verb": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Take one emotional line from a script or film. 2) Write three actions aimed at another person: win, hide, corner, comfort or recruit. 3) Run the line three ways and note which action creates behaviour without forcing a result. Usual mistake: Giving five notes at once. One action, one run, one observation.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: The director's read: how Kazan and Lumet read actors
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The director's read: how Kazan and Lumet read actors" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: I do not direct tears or confidence. I give a person something urgent to do to another person, then make the room safe enough for the attempt.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Reading a group: who really decides?
cards.q: What is the hidden-profile trap?
options: Groups repeat shared facts and support initial preferences
Groups discuss unique facts before shared facts, then compare them carefully
Groups always obey the quietest member in the room
cards.why: Stasser and Titus found that common knowledge and initial preference can dominate discussion.

cards.name: Reading a group: who really decides?
cards.q: Which statement best separates champion from economic buyer?
options: The economic buyer is only the daily user of the product and never funds it
The champion advocates internally; the economic buyer owns budget or business risk and final approval
The champion always has the highest title in the company and the biggest team
cards.why: Roles can overlap, but advocacy and financial authority are different jobs.

cards.name: Reading a group: who really decides?
cards.q: What is the best first-five-minute signal of decision power?
options: Who has the newest laptop and the most impressive setup
Who speaks longest and interrupts the most people
cards.why: Eyes and commitment behaviour are stronger clues than talk time or props. Verify with the approval-path question.

cards.name: Reading a group: who really decides?
cards.q: Drill "The five-minute room map": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) From memory, draw the people in your last meeting and mark who looked at whom. 2) Give each person one power base: title, expertise, information, relationship, reward, coercion or budget. 3) Write one question that reveals the approval path without asking, "Who is the real boss?" Usual mistake: Confusing quiet with weak and loud with powerful. Power is what someone can change when resisted.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Reading a group: who really decides?
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Reading a group: who really decides?" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: The decider is not always the loudest or highest. I watch who gets looked at, who can veto, who carries the risk and who can make the room wait.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Subtext: reading what isn't said
cards.q: What did Mehrabian and Ferris actually study?
options: Business calls and lie detection across ordinary deals
All communication across cultures and every channel
cards.why: The result concerns narrow attitude and liking judgments when channels conflict, not a general communication law.

cards.name: Subtext: reading what isn't said
cards.q: A client says "interesting" after a four-second pause. Best first move?
cards.why: Keep the inference reversible. Ask a question that distinguishes praise, concern and budget.

cards.name: Subtext: reading what isn't said
cards.q: In Pinker, Nowak and Lee, why can indirectness help?
options: It removes every conflict from the exchange
It guarantees agreement from the listener
cards.why: Indirectness can let a cooperative listener accept the intent while leaving an adversarial listener less direct evidence.

cards.name: Subtext: reading what isn't said
cards.q: Drill "Subtext ledger": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Write one sentence you heard today exactly as said. 2) Mark the pause, repair, omission and power relation around it. 3) Write one neutral question that lets the speaker correct your read. Usual mistake: Treating your first inference as the truth. A read is a question with evidence attached.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Subtext: reading what isn't said
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Subtext: reading what isn't said" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I do not translate a pause into a verdict. I write down what happened, then ask the question that lets the other person correct me."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Reading across cultures
cards.q: What is the safest use of a culture framework?
options: A replacement for asking direct questions
A fixed personality diagnosis for this client
cards.why: Meyer's scales and Hall's context are maps. Individual, role and organisation can overturn the first read.

cards.name: Reading across cultures
cards.q: Why is Hofstede risky when applied to one client?
options: It measures only language and nothing else
cards.why: The ecological fallacy warns against projecting country-level relationships onto people or organisations.

cards.name: Reading across cultures
cards.q: A Kenyan partner is warm but has not signed. Best read?
options: The deal is certainly dead already
Warmth proves the price is accepted without another step
cards.why: Relationship can be a condition for business, not proof that the commercial decision is complete.

cards.name: Reading across cultures
cards.q: Drill "Four-lens reset": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Name the likely culture cue without treating it as fact. 2) Add the individual, organisation and role as corrections. 3) Ask one question about feedback, trust or decisions and record the answer. Usual mistake: Using a country label to excuse poor listening. Cultural knowledge should make you more curious, not more certain.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Reading across cultures
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Reading across cultures" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "A culture map tells me what to ask about. It does not tell me who the person is. I test the map, then I listen."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Boss fight: read a real meeting
cards.q: What is the first question in a boss-fight meeting read?
options: Who has the nicest title and longest tenure?
Who is most charismatic and persuasive in the room?
cards.why: Frame the decision before interpreting motives. Otherwise you map a meeting without knowing what it can change.

cards.name: Boss fight: read a real meeting
cards.q: Billy Beane and the scouts mainly disagree about...
options: Whether baseball exists as a professional sport
Who should speak first in this meeting
cards.why: The conflict is over the evaluation frame: reputation and appearance versus the measurable problem Oakland must solve.

cards.name: Boss fight: read a real meeting
cards.q: Why set rewatch=True on this stop?
options: To replace the evidence table with a film montage
To hide the meeting scene from the reader
cards.why: The renderer adds every scene in this file as a warm-up before the final boss-fight read.

cards.name: Boss fight: read a real meeting
cards.q: Drill "Meeting playback": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Watch three minutes with sound and mark who changes the frame. 2) Write each speaker's likely hunger and power, with a question mark. 3) Name the next decision, owner, evidence and date. Usual mistake: Explaining everyone psychologically without checking the decision mechanics. A room read must predict what happens next.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Boss fight: read a real meeting
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Boss fight: read a real meeting" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I do not only read the presenter. I read who needs what, who can block it, what the room is avoiding and what decision will prove me wrong."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The prep kit: one line, three stories, three questions, one ask
cards.q: What is the best preparation for a flexible call?
options: One line plus a small bank
A complete script for every turn
cards.why: A short map protects listening; a full script competes with it.

cards.name: The prep kit: one line, three stories, three questions, one ask
cards.q: What did coherent narratives improve in Cohn-Sheehy et al. 2021?
cards.why: Narrative coherence helped participants recall temporally separated events.

cards.name: The prep kit: one line, three stories, three questions, one ask
cards.q: What did accuracy-focused retelling improve?
cards.why: Dudukovic, Marsh and Tversky found the accuracy goal produced more detailed, accurate later recall.

cards.name: The prep kit: one line, three stories, three questions, one ask
cards.q: Drill "The four-corner prep": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Write your one-line intro in 15 words or fewer. 2) List three true stories as problem, proof and lesson; write three open questions. 3) Circle one ask that is specific, small and easy to refuse. Usual mistake: Bringing a speech into the room. If the other person says something surprising, follow it and abandon the prepared route.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: The prep kit: one line, three stories, three questions, one ask
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The prep kit: one line, three stories, three questions, one ask" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: I do not script the room. I bring a clear spine, three true stories and better questions, then I earn the next step.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Voice: pace and the pause
cards.q: What is the safest default for a complex decision?
cards.why: Rate effects are conditional. Moderate variation protects both energy and comprehension.

cards.name: Voice: pace and the pause
cards.q: What did the 2025 synthesis find about faster speech?
options: It has no measurable effect in any study
It always persuades more, whatever the message
cards.why: Across six studies, the relationship was curvilinear.

cards.name: Voice: pace and the pause
cards.q: Where should a useful pause go?
cards.why: Use breath and silence around the word that changes the meaning.

cards.name: Voice: pace and the pause
cards.q: Drill "The three-speed take": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Record a 20-second explanation at your natural pace. 2) Record it again, adding one breath before the key word and one full beat after it. 3) Record a third version with a quicker opening, a slower decision sentence and a normal ask. Usual mistake: Turning every pause into a dramatic stare. A useful pause is short, placed and followed by a clear word.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Voice: pace and the pause
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Voice: pace and the pause" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: I do not slow down to look important. I give important words enough room to arrive.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Voice: pitch and landing the line
cards.q: What did the lower-pitch experiments actually show?
cards.why: The evidence is about perception and choice, not an intrinsic ability created by pitch.

cards.name: Voice: pitch and landing the line
cards.q: What is the safest way to sound settled?
options: Force your larynx down to sound low
cards.why: Do not strain. Support the voice you have and land the content word.

cards.name: Voice: pitch and landing the line
cards.q: What is the careful verdict on the Thatcher story?
options: It is entirely invented, with no coaching
One lower pitch explains her election
cards.why: BBC and the Independent support coaching and presentation changes, not a single-cause career story.

cards.name: Voice: pitch and landing the line
cards.q: Drill "The landing ladder": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Choose one honest closing sentence and mark its final content word. 2) Say it three times: rising, level and gently falling, without changing volume. 3) Keep the version that sounds complete and leaves a turn for the listener. Usual mistake: Dropping pitch theatrically or squeezing the throat. Authority is not a vocal costume.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Voice: pitch and landing the line
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Voice: pitch and landing the line" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: I do not borrow someone else's voice. I make my own clear enough that the last word can stand.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The body: walk, stance, stillness
cards.q: What did Ranehill et al. 2015 find after a larger replication?
options: No hormone or behavioural effect, but felt power rose
Hormone and risk effects remained large
No participant reported any change in any hormone, behaviour, or feeling measure
cards.why: The replication did not reproduce hormones or risk behaviour, while self-reported power still rose.

cards.name: The body: walk, stance, stillness
cards.q: In Johnstone's status work, status is best treated as...
options: A changing behaviour in a relationship
A costume code for actors in every scene
cards.why: Status is something people do in interaction, and it shifts with the partner and moment.

cards.name: The body: walk, stance, stillness
cards.q: What is the practical replacement for power posing?
options: Spread out until others yield and accept your supposed dominance
Use a pose to alter testosterone before every meeting
Prepare the first action and make your body easy to read
cards.why: Use posture as a readiness cue, not as a biochemical or social cheat code.

cards.name: The body: walk, stance, stillness
cards.q: Drill "Arrive, plant, decide": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Walk 20 steps toward a fixed point at an unhurried pace. 2) Plant your feet, loosen your hands, and hold a natural stance for three breaths. 3) Say one difficult sentence after a silent two-count, then replay it with one unnecessary gesture removed. Usual mistake: Turning stillness into a frozen stare or a dominance pose. Stay responsive to the person and the room.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: The body: walk, stance, stillness
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The body: walk, stance, stillness" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: I do not power-pose. I arrive, plant, and let the decision land.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Calm under pressure
cards.q: What is the most defensible claim about physiological sighs?
options: They replace emergency treatment and professional help in a real crisis
Structured practice may reduce arousal and improve mood
cards.why: The 2023 trial is promising, but it studied structured daily practice and does not justify a cure claim.

cards.name: Calm under pressure
cards.q: Jamieson's arousal reappraisal asks people to...
options: Treat arousal as useful for the task
Pretend the task is not stressful and ignore the signal
cards.why: Participants were told to interpret stress arousal as functional and adaptive.

cards.name: Calm under pressure
cards.q: What does an audience usually need first in a crisis?
options: A fact, next action and standard
A long explanation of your feelings before any action
cards.why: A usable sequence lets people act. Calm is process made audible.

cards.name: Calm under pressure
cards.q: Drill "The useful arousal card": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Take two easy physiological sighs, without forcing the breath. 2) Say silently: "This is mobilisation, not a verdict. What does the task require?" 3) Answer aloud in three parts: fact, next action, standard. Usual mistake: Trying to look relaxed while speaking in foggy generalities. Calm is clarity, not cosmetic stillness.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Calm under pressure
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Calm under pressure" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: Calm is not no adrenaline. Calm is giving the adrenaline a job.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Warmth and humour
cards.q: When appropriate humour lands, what does it often signal?
options: That the speaker knows every person and every norm
cards.why: Bitterly, Brooks and Schweitzer link successful humour to perceived confidence and competence.

cards.name: Warmth and humour
cards.q: What is the safer business target for a joke?
cards.why: Self-directed, low-stakes humour lowers the cost for others. Targeted humour can expose poor judgement.

cards.name: Warmth and humour
cards.q: What is Danny Ocean's ethical move worth copying?
options: Hide the real plan until they commit to the whole pitch
Make the other person feel capable and free to choose
cards.why: Copy invitation, agency and shared attention, not the con.

cards.name: Warmth and humour
cards.q: Drill "The permission ladder": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Write one neutral observation about the shared situation, not the person. 2) Try it once with a trusted friend and notice whether the laugh is easy or forced. 3) After the line, ask a genuine question and give the light back. Usual mistake: Using humour to cover anxiety, sell too fast, or test whether a stranger will tolerate disrespect.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Warmth and humour
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Warmth and humour" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: My joke is an invitation, not a test. If the room cannot safely join it, I do not make it.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The long take: monologues
cards.q: What is the most useful long-take sequence for a pitch?
options: Claim, resistance, changed frame, next action
Jokes, credentials, urgency, discount, then a pressure tactic
Features, price, close, then a rushed ask and a final reminder
cards.why: A useful pitch changes the listener's question, then lands on one honest action.

cards.name: The long take: monologues
cards.q: What did Green and Brock study as transportation?
options: Speaking speed during sales calls and meetings
Whether every story is remembered word for word after a week
Absorption in imagery, emotion and attention during a narrative
cards.why: Transportation is the experience of entering a narrative world through attention, imagery and affect.

cards.name: The long take: monologues
cards.q: What is the ethical limit of borrowing a coercive monologue?
options: Never use a story in business, even when the evidence is clear
Copy the structure, not humiliation or false scarcity
Copy the insult if the room is quiet and the buyer seems receptive
cards.why: Form can be studied without importing coercion. Evidence and a reversible next step keep the pitch honest.

cards.name: The long take: monologues
cards.q: Drill "The four-beat long take": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Write one problem, one cost and one image from a real client. 2) Speak it as frame, pressure, turn, landing, with a pause before the turn. 3) Record the same take at half speed and remove one sentence that does no work. Usual mistake: Adding drama instead of changing meaning. If the turn does not alter the listener's question, rewrite it.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: The long take: monologues
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The long take: monologues" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: I do not make a pitch longer to sound important. I give it a turn, then I leave the room a next step.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: George Newman and the off switch
cards.q: What does Snyder mean by self-monitoring?
options: Never changing your behaviour, even when the room gives new information
Observing and regulating your displayed behaviour using social cues
Reading minds from body language and treating the guess as a fact
cards.why: Snyder studied self-observation and self-control guided by cues about social appropriateness.

cards.name: George Newman and the off switch
cards.q: What did the emotional-labor meta-analysis associate with surface acting?
options: A guaranteed promotion from displaying the right emotion at work
Better sleep in every workplace after a demanding customer interaction
cards.why: The result is an association across studies, not a claim that every display causes harm.

cards.name: George Newman and the off switch
cards.q: What is the off switch for?
options: Returning to chosen, unperformed recovery and relationships
Hiding all emotion from clients and trusted people after the meeting ends
Winning every interaction by keeping the persona switched on
cards.why: A persona is a tool. The switch protects recovery and keeps the role from becoming an identity.

cards.name: George Newman and the off switch
cards.q: Drill "The switch rehearsal": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Name the room and the legitimate purpose of your persona. 2) Choose one voice, body and warmth behaviour, then breathe out and label the feeling underneath. 3) Practise an exit: remove the jacket, unclench the jaw, write one honest sentence to yourself. Usual mistake: Calling every private feeling a truth that must be shared. The off switch is for recovery and choice, not theatrical confession.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: George Newman and the off switch
cards.q: Page closed: explain "George Newman and the off switch" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: George Newman is my jacket, not my skin. I put him on for the room, then I come home as Kevin.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Boss fight: a room of strangers
cards.q: What should you carry into a room of strangers?
options: One line, three stories, three questions and one ask
A full service catalogue with every technology, price and case study ready
A rule to talk until someone agrees, even when they are looking for an exit
cards.why: The prep kit reduces wandering while leaving room to read and update.

cards.name: Boss fight: a room of strangers
cards.q: What is the ethical response when a stranger does not reciprocate?
options: Keep talking until they comply, even after the conversation has clearly cooled
Increase urgency and explain why they should decide before leaving
Land cleanly and give them an easy exit
cards.why: Warmth includes consent and an exit. Lack of reciprocity is data, not a challenge to overcome.

cards.name: Boss fight: a room of strangers
cards.q: When should George Newman switch off?
options: Only after every person has approved the pitch and agreed to a follow-up
After the agreed interaction, during recovery and with trusted people
Never, because consistency proves confidence in every room and relationship
cards.why: The persona is a tool. Recovery and unperformed relationships keep the tool from becoming an identity.

cards.name: Boss fight: a room of strangers
cards.q: Drill "The stranger-room rehearsal": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Say your one line while standing level, breathing out before the final word. 2) Role-play three replies: eager, guarded and distracted. Ask one question and give each person an exit. 3) Deliver the 30-second long take, pause, name the next step, and physically switch off. Usual mistake: Treating every pause as rejection or every smile as buying intent. Read reciprocity over time, not one cue.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Boss fight: a room of strangers
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Boss fight: a room of strangers" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: I enter prepared, read without pretending I know, tell one useful story, ask permission, and leave George Newman at the door.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Known for one thing: the website guy
cards.q: What made Ruddy legible to Paramount?
options: A long list of unrelated skills
cards.why: The sources support his cost, speed and delivery reputation. A portable identity made him easy to choose.

cards.name: Known for one thing: the website guy
cards.q: What is the careful version of the weak-tie finding?
options: Weak ties always beat strong ties
Weak ties can bridge groups, with effects varying by context
cards.why: Granovetter gives the bridge idea; Rajkumar et al. add a nonlinear, industry-dependent causal result.

cards.name: Known for one thing: the website guy
cards.q: Which is the strongest positioning line for Kevin?
options: I build safari websites that win bookings
I do websites, apps, AI and many other things
cards.why: It names a client, a useful result and a repeatable pattern.

cards.name: Known for one thing: the website guy
cards.q: Drill "The one-line test": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Write client, costly problem and measurable result in one sentence. 2) Remove tools, credentials and adjectives until the sentence still has a clear win. 3) Say it to one friend and ask what they would tell someone else about you. Usual mistake: Choosing a niche because it sounds stylish. Choose the problem you can repeatedly solve.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Known for one thing: the website guy
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Known for one thing: the website guy" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: I am not a general digital agency. I am the website person for wildlife and safari brands, and I can show you the booking problem I fix.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The one-minute pitch
cards.q: What belongs first in Kevin's one-minute pitch?
cards.why: Lead with the listener's problem. Proof and promise follow.

cards.name: The one-minute pitch
cards.q: What did Huang and Pearce mean by investor gut feel?
options: A fixed checklist used by every investor
cards.why: Their study describes dynamic emotion-cognition under extreme uncertainty, not magic.

cards.name: The one-minute pitch
cards.q: After the small next step, what should Kevin do?
options: Keep adding features until they agree
Stop and let the listener respond
cards.why: The pitch ends where a real conversation starts.

cards.name: The one-minute pitch
cards.q: Drill "Four beats, one breath": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Write the listener's costly problem in twelve words. 2) Add one proof and one changed outcome. 3) End with a small ask and practise stopping for three seconds. Usual mistake: Answering an imagined objection before the listener has shown interest. Let their question choose the next beat.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: The one-minute pitch
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The one-minute pitch" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: The pitch is not my speech. It is the first question I make easy for you to ask.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Favours and gifts, done right
cards.q: What makes the Godfather favour an anti-model?
options: The request is backed by coercive power
cards.why: The problem is not reciprocity. It is that refusal is unsafe and the debt is enforced.

cards.name: Favours and gifts, done right
cards.q: What is the careful status of the Ben Franklin effect?
options: A finding with no study at all
cards.why: Jecker and Landy published the classic 1969 experiment. Its narrow evidence does not justify a guaranteed tactic.

cards.name: Favours and gifts, done right
cards.q: What should guide a professional gift?
options: How much future debt it creates
How impressive it looks to you
cards.why: Gift research finds a recurring giver-recipient mismatch. Start with their use.

cards.name: Favours and gifts, done right
cards.q: Drill "Open-loop reciprocity": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Choose one useful thing you can give without resentment. 2) Write a request with cost, reason and an easy no. 3) Write the thank-you you will send even if the answer is no. Usual mistake: Giving something unwanted, then silently charging interest. Ask what would actually help.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Favours and gifts, done right
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Favours and gifts, done right" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: I can help with that. You do not owe me anything, and if I ask for a favour later you can say no without damaging the relationship.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Waking dormant ties
cards.q: What did the dormant-ties study compare?
options: Advice from dormant and current ties
Sales from gifts to sales from pitches
cards.why: Executive MBA students consulted dormant and current contacts on an important work project.

cards.name: Waking dormant ties
cards.q: What should open a reconnection message?
cards.why: Context lowers awkwardness and gives the person a reason to reply.

cards.name: Waking dormant ties
cards.q: What is the ethical boundary in the Ocean's Eleven lesson?
options: Use history with a safe refusal
Use history to pressure a yes
Never contact anyone from the past
cards.why: Shared history can support a respectful ask, but it cannot make refusal unsafe.

cards.name: Waking dormant ties
cards.q: Drill "The warm re-entry": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Write the shared context and one detail you genuinely remember. 2) Write your current update in two sentences, with no achievement parade. 3) Ask one bounded question and add an easy no or no-reply option. Usual mistake: Pretending the silence did not happen. Acknowledge the gap lightly and give the person a reason that is about them as well as you.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Waking dormant ties
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Waking dormant ties" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: We have been out of touch, so I will not pretend this is casual. I remembered your work on X, and I would value your view on one specific question. No pressure if now is not a good time.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The follow-up system
cards.q: What did the HBR audit find among companies that replied within 30 days?
cards.why: The reported average was 42 hours. The study does not establish a universal five-minute law.

cards.name: The follow-up system
cards.q: What belongs in Kevin's people CRM?
options: Context, promise, date, and permission to stop
A script that handles every possible objection for you
cards.why: The system stores human context and agreed next actions, with an exit condition.

cards.name: The follow-up system
cards.q: Joe Girard's 250 figure is best treated as...
cards.why: The Hall of Fame account says it came from Girard's informal polling, so use it as a story, not a law.

cards.name: The follow-up system
cards.q: Drill "The seven-field card": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Write one person's name, context, and current problem. 2) Write one useful thing you can deliver and a date. 3) Add the stop condition: what counts as a no or a pause? Usual mistake: Turning a person into a lead score. The card is for remembering promises and consent.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: The follow-up system
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The follow-up system" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I do not chase people. I keep promises, add something useful, and make the next step easy to decline."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Working a room
cards.q: What did the instrumented mixer reveal?
options: Friends made about half of encounters
Nobody met anyone outside their existing network
cards.why: The average guest had 14 encounters and friends accounted for a disproportionate half.

cards.name: Working a room
cards.q: What is the best entry to a group?
options: Stand silently and wait for someone to rescue you
Use a host, topic, or mutual contact as a bridge
cards.why: A bridge makes the interruption legible and gives both people a reason to continue.

cards.name: Working a room
cards.q: In Cheng et al., prestige differed from dominance because prestige targets were...
cards.why: Both could increase influence, but prestige targets were viewed as likable while dominance targets were not.

cards.name: Working a room
cards.q: Drill "The edge entry": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Name a room you will enter and one honest bridge into it. 2) Write one question that fits the room, not your pitch. 3) Write your exit: one introduction or useful link, then leave. Usual mistake: Treating the room as a hunt for status. The aim is a better-connected room after you leave.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Working a room
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Working a room" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I am not trying to work the whole room. I am trying to leave one small bridge stronger than I found it."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The 48 Laws worth knowing, decoded
cards.q: What does a historical anecdote prove?
options: A story in a particular context
A replicated experiment across many modern workplaces
cards.why: Anecdotes can suggest mechanisms, but they do not establish universal effects.

cards.name: The 48 Laws worth knowing, decoded
cards.q: Which status route was liked more in Cheng et al.?
cards.why: Prestige and dominance could both increase influence, but prestige targets were liked.

cards.name: The 48 Laws worth knowing, decoded
cards.q: What did the influence-tactics meta-analysis find about pressure?
options: It was always the best tactic in every workplace
It was negatively related to outcomes
cards.why: Across the meta-analysis, pressure was negatively related to task and relationship outcomes.

cards.name: The 48 Laws worth knowing, decoded
cards.q: Drill "The five-pass decoder": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Choose one law or power move and state its mechanism. 2) List the red flag and the defence. 3) Write the honest version without a script for controlling anyone. Usual mistake: Admiring the move before asking who loses. Every tactic has a target and a cost.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: The 48 Laws worth knowing, decoded
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The 48 Laws worth knowing, decoded" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Greene gives me warning labels, not lines. I want the mechanism, the red flag, and the honest replacement."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Boss fight: the follow-up week
cards.q: What is the boss-fight score?
options: How many people were forced to answer you
Promises kept and next steps clarified
cards.why: The useful unit is a clearer next step, a useful bridge, a pause, or a clean no.

cards.name: Boss fight: the follow-up week
cards.q: Why does the cadence evidence need a caveat?
options: It is based on vendor observational data
It proves one schedule for all relationships
cards.why: The report is vendor observational data and does not prove a universal schedule.

cards.name: Boss fight: the follow-up week
cards.q: On Friday, what should Kevin do with repeated silence?
options: Invent an objection and answer it
cards.why: A stop rule protects the prospect and turns silence into a decision about your process.

cards.name: Boss fight: the follow-up week
cards.q: Drill "The five-day card": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Choose three prospects and label the relationship type, not just the lead temperature. 2) Write Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday actions. 3) Add the review fields: promise kept, reply, next step, pause, or no. Usual mistake: Treating activity as progress. A full week of touches can still be a failure if the other person never had a real choice.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Boss fight: the follow-up week
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Boss fight: the follow-up week" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "My network is not a pile of names. It is a set of promises I can keep, bridges I can make, and no answers I can respect."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Influence vs manipulation: the disclosure test
cards.q: What is the disclosure test looking for?
options: Whether the listener agrees without checking the claim
Whether the appeal survives being made visible
cards.why: Disclosure is a practical diagnostic. It exposes a hidden pressure or shows that the reasons can stand in daylight.

cards.name: Influence vs manipulation: the disclosure test
cards.q: Sunstein's centre of gravity is that manipulation...
options: Uses any emotional language, even when truthful
cards.why: Sunstein distinguishes manipulation from coercion and deception while centring reflective choice.

cards.name: Influence vs manipulation: the disclosure test
cards.q: Cialdini's ethical influence requires...
options: A secret advantage hidden in the framing
cards.why: The same principles can be used ethically or dishonestly. Long-term trust is the check.

cards.name: Influence vs manipulation: the disclosure test
cards.q: Drill "Daylight audit": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Write the decision you want and your own upside. 2) List one material downside or alternative the listener should know. 3) Read the appeal aloud and mark the sentence that would be hardest to say openly. Usual mistake: Turning disclosure into a performance while still hiding the relevant cost.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Influence vs manipulation: the disclosure test
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Influence vs manipulation: the disclosure test" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "If I cannot explain what I am doing, what I gain and where you can say no, I am not influencing you honestly."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Belfort, decoded
cards.q: What is the safest reading of Belfort's straight-line pitch?
options: A narrowing sequence that can suppress due diligence
A method for making any investment safe and profitable
cards.why: The mechanism can hold attention, but a buyer still needs evidence, incentives and time.

cards.name: Belfort, decoded
cards.q: What restitution amount appears in the court record?
cards.why: The court record gives the restitution order as 110,362,993.87 dollars. The SEC settlement lists other amounts for different obligations.

cards.name: Belfort, decoded
cards.q: What is the best defence to urgency?
options: Ask for a bigger discount before you decide
cards.why: Time, documents and an independent check widen the frame that a pressure pitch narrows.

cards.name: Belfort, decoded
cards.q: Drill "The pause button": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Take a famous high-energy pitch and remove its certainty words. 2) Write the missing evidence a buyer would need. 3) Add a sentence granting time to compare and decline. Usual mistake: Copying the rhythm of a pressure pitch while calling it ethical because the product is legitimate.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Belfort, decoded
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Belfort, decoded" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "A straight line is for a clean explanation, not a trapped buyer. I leave room for evidence, comparison and no."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Barry Seal: useful to everyone, loyal to no one
cards.q: What does the historical record most securely show about Seal?
options: He was only a CIA pilot, not an informant
He was a DEA informant with cartel access
cards.why: The record supports his smuggling, DEA cooperation and 1986 murder. The film expands and simplifies the CIA story.

cards.name: Barry Seal: useful to everyone, loyal to no one
cards.q: What is the safest lesson for Kevin?
options: Serve every powerful person without asking questions
Set a scope, conflict rule and clear allegiance
Stay ambiguous to keep options open
cards.why: Useful expertise becomes trustworthy when people know whom you represent and what you will not carry across boundaries.

cards.name: Barry Seal: useful to everyone, loyal to no one
cards.q: The CIA evidence around Seal is best described as...
options: A confirmed lifelong CIA recruitment from the start of his career
Documented around a 1984 operation, with the larger story contested
cards.why: The declassified report documents the 1984 operation. It does not establish the film's complete CIA mythology.

cards.name: Barry Seal: useful to everyone, loyal to no one
cards.q: Drill "Boundary before brilliance": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Name one capability a client needs from you. 2) Name the information or access you must not carry between clients. 3) Write the sentence you will use when a request crosses that line. Usual mistake: Waiting until a crisis to decide whom you represent.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Barry Seal: useful to everyone, loyal to no one
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Barry Seal: useful to everyone, loyal to no one" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Being useful opens doors. Being reliable keeps them open. I tell each client which door I am standing in."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: When the mask eats the man
cards.q: What is the safest use of a persona?
options: Use it with a named exit and a values check
Treat it as your permanent identity
cards.why: Roles can help. The danger is forgetting they are roles and letting their rewards choose for you.

cards.name: When the mask eats the man
cards.q: What did Tice's research suggest?
options: Every performance becomes a disorder or diagnosis
cards.why: Tice found stronger self-concept effects for identical behaviour performed publicly. That supports a mechanism, not an inevitable tragedy.

cards.name: When the mask eats the man
cards.q: What is the final calibration of the guide?
options: Read people as fixed types before asking questions
Trust a first impression if it feels vivid
Read, ask, verify and keep an exit
cards.why: The guide is a loop: observe, ask, update, act honestly and retain the ability to stop.

cards.name: When the mask eats the man
cards.q: Drill "The off switch": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Name the role you used today and the reward it gave you. 2) Write the behaviour you will stop when the meeting ends. 3) Ask one trusted person what you look like when the role is running too hot. Usual mistake: Calling a mask your personality because other people rewarded it.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: When the mask eats the man
cards.q: Page closed: explain "When the mask eats the man" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "George Newman gets me through the door. Kevin decides what I do once I am inside."
cards.label: Say it in the room
